items.extracted_excerpt: Introducing Sakana AI’s Security Research Group
items.extracted_text_for_analysis: （＊日本語は英文の後に） Sakana AI is launching the Security Research Group, an independent R&D team studying collective, AI-driven cyber defense and the security and safety of AI itself. Our research starts from the idea that intelligence and resilience emerge from collectives, like a school of fish rather than a single swimmer. As a company building frontier AI, we also believe we share responsibility for the security of the society that uses it. Separate from our commercial business, the group’s mission is to serve the public interest: publishing research, reproducible benchmarks, and practical guidelines, and working with government, industry, and academia on research to improve cybersecurity. What We Are Seeing Frontier AI’s ability to find flaws in software is growing, and the number of disclosed flaws is climbing. NIST reports that CVE submissions rose 263% between 2020 and 2025, and that early 2026 ran nearly a third above the same period a year earlier. JVN iPedia, which provides vulnerability information in Japanese, also registered nearly twice as many entries in the latest quarter as a year earlier, most of them from the NVD. AI is widely suspected to play a part, though there is still more to confirm: FIRST points to AI-assisted discovery alongside administrative factors, and NIST staff say AI-based discovery tools have added to their workload. Japan’s government now treats the trend as a national security matter. The strain is already showing. NIST has stopped routine analysis of older records and now prioritizes flaws known to be exploited. Japan’s financial regulators have asked institutions to treat the response as a management issue, with top management directly involved. Flaws are being found at machine speed and fixed at organizational speed, and we suspect the people in between are the ones bearing the cost. The other side is changing too. Attackers are using AI agents, running intrusions against many targets at once. And AI systems are themselves becoming targets: NICT recorded more probing aimed at AI service endpoints in the first quarter of 2026. Why Faster Response Is Not Enough Faster triage and patching are necessary, but patching systems already in operation will not be enough to bring overall risk down. CISA’s review of two fiscal years finds that many attackers exploit well-known, straightforward weaknesses, with input validation and memory safety flaws the most dependable ways in, and it calls for eliminating persistent, preventable weaknesses. NICT’s recent alert on attacks against the servers behind mobile apps names the same kinds of weakness, such as missing authorization checks and unvalidated input. The FBI’s account of the AI-agent intrusions lists SSRF, IDOR, missing API authentication and injection. Even if AI makes finding these flaws faster, if the same weaknesses keep being introduced into software and architecture, the work is likely to keep growing. That is why we believe the lasting answer lies upstream, in the development process of systems, AI included. Instead of chasing flaws after release, the aim is to keep them from arising at the design and build stage, or to remove them there. Japan’s government-wide package points the same way, asking software vendors to apply secure-by-design principles and to use advanced AI across development to find and fix vulnerabilities early. Four layers of defense, from upstream to downstream: the quality of each product, the design and configuration of the system, operation and patching, and detection and response. The Security Research Group works across all four, with its long-term weight on the upstream two. Quality Is Where Japan Can Lead We propose to treat this as a question of quality. Finding and fixing vulnerabilities may be seen as a special task that security specialists carry out separately, after the product is built. We would rather see it as part of the quality a product is expected to have, and raise that quality at the source. Japan may be well placed to lead on this. Japanese manufacturing built its worldwide reputation on quality, and that tradition is part of how Japan’s products have long been valued. Rethinking quality through the security of software is a challenge, and also a chance to raise Japan’s profile. AI can help here as well. The same capability that finds flaws in finished systems can be turned into a way of checking quality at every step of design, building and operation, and we will use it to the fullest on the defending side. If the expertise of excellent human reviewers can be built into AI agents, quality could be assured at a scale and depth that were hard to reach before, and the flaws found today could teach us not to build the same flaws tomorrow. That gives defenders reason for hope. Security Is Must-Be Quality The Kano model, widely used in quality management, sorts quality into three kinds by how they relate to user satisfaction: attractive quality, which delights when present; one-dimensional quality, which satisfies in step with how well it is met; and must-be quality. Must-be quality goes unnoticed when it is present and causes strong dissatisfaction only when it is missing. Safety is a classic example, and security is another; because they are taken for granted and so rarely asked for explicitly, both are easily left out of the definition of quality altogether. That is why they have to be treated as quality requirements from the start and built in, rather than inspected for at the end. Keeping quality means working to never introduce the gaps that lead to incidents, in the software we run and in AI systems themselves. Safety and security are must-be qualities in the Kano model: meeting them never lifts users above neutral, but falling short causes strong dissatisfaction. Conceptual sketch after Kano et al. (1984). Japan’s Constraints Responding to AI-era vulnerabilities is hard in Japan, most likely for reasons like those set out in public documents, including the request from the Financial Services Agency and the Bank of Japan. - Outsourced operations: Many organizations entrust system maintenance to vendors, so whether patching is covered by the maintenance contract, and who is responsible for what, needs to be clear in advance. - Technical debt: Legacy systems and incomplete asset inventories can make it hard to tell which flaws apply, and harder still to fix them. - Limited staff: Substantially expanding IT staff in the short term is not realistic, so the expertise that exists has to be focused where it matters most. Under these conditions, simply adding people will not keep up. We see these difficulties as structural, or design, problems to solve. The fewer flaws a product has, the less vendor coordination, patch windows and emergency staffing it needs. items.extracted_title: GPT-Live 1.1 now available on AI Gateway - Vercel
items.extracted_excerpt: Run OpenAI's GPT-Live 1.1 voice sessions through Vercel AI Gateway with one API key: no provider account, per-second billing, and usage on every session.
items.extracted_text_for_analysis: GPT-Live 1.1 from OpenAI is now available on AI Gateway. GPT-Live 1.1 is a full-duplex voice model, so it listens while it speaks and a caller can pause, interrupt, or add detail mid-reply. Compared with the previous GPT-Live model, it transcribes speech more accurately and keeps a more consistent accent and voice across languages. It uses the same Live endpoint and client delegation, so an existing GPT-Live integration only needs the new model ID. Copy link to headingSimple example without delegation Run openai/gpt-live-1.1 by itself: import { createOpenAI } from '@ai-sdk/openai'; const live = createOpenAI({ apiKey: process.env.AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY, baseURL: 'https://ai-gateway.vercel.sh/v1',}).experimental_realtime('openai/gpt-live-1.1', { api: 'live' }); const { url, headers } = await live.getServerWebSocketConfig(); send(live.serializeClientEvent({ type: 'session-start', config: { instructions: 'You are a helpful voice assistant.' },})); Copy link to headingDelegate work and keep talking Turn on client delegation, and use the session instructions to tell GPT-Live 1.1 when to ask for help. It asks by sending delegation-created. Answer with any text model on AI Gateway and return the result on the commentary channel for GPT-Live to speak. This example uses openai/gpt-6.2-sol and builds on the session above: send(live.serializeClientEvent({ type: 'session-start', config: { instructions: 'Ask the application for help with order questions.', providerOptions: { openai: { delegation: { type: 'client' } } }, },})); async function handleDelegation({ delegationId }) { const { text } = await generateText({ model: 'openai/gpt-6.2-sol', // Any text model prompt: conversationContext, }); send(live.serializeClientEvent({ type: 'context-append', delegationId, content: text, providerOptions: { openai: { channel: 'commentary' } }, }));} Your application controls delegated work and its permissions, confirmations, and cancellation. Delegated model requests are billed separately through AI Gateway, and voice-session usage continues while they run. These snippets omit the WebSocket connection, event parsing, transcript assembly, audio streaming, and shutdown. See the GPT-Live guide for connection setup, audio streaming, and complete examples. Try GPT-Live 1.1 in the model playground. AI Gateway provides a unified API for calling models, tracking usage and cost, and configuring retries, failover, and performance optimizations for higher-than-provider uptime. It includes built-in custom reporting, Zero Data Retention support, budgets for API keys, routing rules, and more. AI Gateway reflects provider pricing with no markup and does not charge a platform fee on inference, including on Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) requests. You can view all models available on AI Gateway.
